articles.text: On Saturday, May 6th, much of the world’s attention was on London where Charles III was coronated as the king of England and his wife, Camilla, was crowned queen of England. Charles is the 41st British monarch since William the Conqueror took control of the land back in 1066. Although the power to rule in England resides in Parliament, the king is far from a primarily ceremonial figure. The British monarch has a great many powers and responsibilities. A recent Reader’s Digest article lists 27 of them: Serve as king of England, Scotland, Northern Ireland, Wales as well as the 14 nations that make up the “Commonwealth realm” • Choose to rule or abdicate • Serve as head of the Commonwealth of Nations • Pick the prime minister • Appoint members to the House of Lords • Appoint Supreme Court justices • Initiate the process of “forming a government” • Open Parliament each year • Kick off parliamentary business • Legitimize laws • Summon the prime minister • End the parliamentary session • Open Welsh lawmaking sessions and ratify its legislation • Open Scotland’s parliamentary session • Ratify the laws of Northern Ireland • Appoint the members of the Privy Council • Approve Privy Council orders and proclamations • Break the law without prosecution • Pardon criminals • Drive without a license • Exceed the speed limit • Travel without a passport • Command the armed forces • Grant knighthoods • Appoint archbishops and bishops to the Church of England (Defender of the Faith), • Own all the dolphins in the United Kingdom. This is an impressive list. It represents much power, simply by right of birth, being bestowed on one person; power given without a vote of parliament or people; authority granted without regard to aptitude, attitude or ability. While Charles’ mother, Queen Elizabeth II, was, at the time of her death, widely respected, the current king has not yet won such a secure place in the hearts of those over whom he rules.
articles.title: Thoughts about a Coronation

articles.text: Congresswoman Barbara Lee shows support for Oakland teachers in front of Oakland City Hall on Thursday, May 4. With 12 days left in the school year, Wednesday, May 10, marks the fifth day of a teacher’s strike in Oakland, with little progress made toward any contract agreement. Congresswoman Barbara Lee – who represents California’s District 12, including Piedmont – rallied a crowd of strikers and supporters in front of Oakland City Hall on Thursday, May 4, after more than 3,000 teachers began picketing due to little progress in settlement negotiations with Oakland Unified School District. Teacher demands included higher wages; more support staff; addressing of gun violence issues; addressing of environmental health issues like lead and asbestos in buildings; and student resources including subsidized transportation, reparations for black students, and district housing for homeless students. While apparently unable to meet all teacher demands, the negotiations include a retroactive 10% raise and a $5,000 one-time bonus for teachers, and a minimum salary raise of at least 13% and as much as 22% for every classroom teacher beginning next year. The offer is expected to cost the school district an historic $70 million more annually. Of the 22 largest California school districts which filed teacher pay data with the state for the 2021-2022 year, Oakland ranked 20th in total pay and 22nd in pay adjusted for cost of living. Among the 55 districts with over 1,000 students in San Francisco and the East Bay, Oakland ranked 54th in pay. The district’s 80 schools remain open for the approximately 35,000 affected students, as Oakland School District taps school staff for teaching and supervision. three days a week. articles.text: Piedmont adults and youth have a wealth of opportunities to explore local volunteer work. Here are just a few. Piedmont Ave. Library The Friends of the Piedmont Avenue Library organization is looking for a treasurer and a social media coordinator. An ideal volunteer for the job of treasurer would have knowledge of accounting and recordkeeping, providing oversight of Friends of PAL finances, taking part in board meetings and presenting financial reports to the library’s board. This volunteer would also pay bills, record bank account activity and analyze cash flow, collect and disburse funds, and prepare data for state and federal filing, and work with the library’s fundraising committee to project cash needs and sources. To apply, email contact@friendsofpal.org with information about your interest and a resume, if available. The social media coordinator will manage digital content on Facebook, Instagram, Twitter for the library’s website, and the library’s monthly newsletter. The library’s social media channel would be updated on a weekly basis with fun, uplifting content, to make sure that the community stays up-to-date about the latest happenings at the library. Harbor House Harbor House is a nonprofit Christian community development organization in Oakland which provides opportunities for children, teens, and families. Volunteer opportunities include virtual tutoring, food distribution, after-school program teachers, and facility maintenance (gardening and handiwork). To apply and learn more, contact the volunteer coordinator (nicole@ hhministries.org), or fill out an application at bit.ly/3YBzu16. Piedmont Center for the Arts Throughout the year, the all-volunteer nonprofit Piedmont Center for the Arts hosts music performances, art exhibits, literary events, public speakers and theater. Volunteers do everything — from production, carpentry, and painting to hosting receptions for events, and handling box office duties. The PCA particularly needs volunteers to staff art exhibits on weekends. To learn more and get involved, email the PCA at info@piedmontcenterforthearts.org, or contact Sue Malick at suemalick@gmail.com. articles.text: Piedmont adults and students gathered in the Ambassador Chris Stevens Library at Piedmont High School on April 26 to meet Lucy Jane Bledsoe, the author of the book No Stopping Us Now, which was the 2023 Readmont book selection. English teacher Beth Black introduced the acclaimed, Berkeley-based author Bledsoe who shared that her story is closely tied to her own high school experiences. In high school, Bledsoe tried to join the Lettermen Club but failed, and faced retaliation in the press and physical intimidation and slander from a high school employee. Ultimately, she prevailed in getting her school to offer girls basketball and found the travails were a great lesson for her. Through these experiences she found her own voice, learned to stick to her truth and be steadfast. Bledsoe confirmed that making change happen and achieving justice is hard. She confessed that as a 17-year-old she was quite naïve. At that time, she thought simply pointing out inequities existed would result in corrections. She quickly learned that this was far from enough and that it took action on many fronts to achieve change, including speaking to the school board, finding mentors, writing to the state paper, building allies, and understanding the law. She has found that facts seem to be less impactful than stories that speak to people’s hearts. Black opened the evening discussion by thanking The Title IX Celebration Committee and the League of Women Voters of Piedmont for acquiring books for the district. She shared how she learned of the book; as part of the curriculum this year in a UC Berkeley history of women in sports class, it resonated with many of the college students. Following Bledsoe’s remarks, there was a rich Question and Answer session which led to discussions of Bledsoe’s writing process and choices, her parents’ fears of her advocacy work as well as their support, where society has and hasn’t made progress since the 1970’s, feminist role models, coming of age, race and intersectionality, high school friendships, the importance of allies, the impact of shaming and slander, representation, and gender equity in areas beyond sports in Piedmont today. The culminating event of Readmont 2023 was a talk in the PHS library with author Lucy Jane Bledsoe. In heartfelt remarks, an adult in the room shared that this was the first book that she had read that captured her own high school experiences in coming into her own sexuality. Bledsoe was very complimentary of the insightful, candid and thoughtful questions and responses from the audience, particularly those from the students. For suggestions of future Readmont selections, contact Beth Black at bblack@piedmont. k12.ca.us.
articles.title: Author of Readmont selection discusses book on Title IX in Piedmont

articles.text: David Gard and Ellen Lee have been co-presidents of the Piedmont Anti-Racism and Diversity Committee (formerly the Piedmont Appreciating Diversity Committee) since August 2022. Gard, who grew up primarily in Missouri and Southern California, moved to Piedmont in 2014, He has two children at Piedmont High School. He joined PADC in 2015 as a city liaison working with city, police department, and fire department staff. With a Ph.D. in clinical psychology from UC Berkeley, Gard has worked as a private psychotherapist and as clinical psychology professor at San Francisco State University, and as director of the school’s Psychology Clinic. “Piedmont is a wonderful community of kind, thoughtful people who, I think, know the reputation Piedmont can have. By and large we all want to make it known how welcoming of diversity we really are,” said Gard. Lee moved to Piedmont from San Francisco 10 years ago. She has three children spanning elementary, middle, and high school. Before she joined the PADC board two years ago, she was a liaison for Wildwood School and co-chaired the PADC School Committee with former president Sheila Leunig. “As an Asian-American person growing up in the Bay, it’s wonderfully multicultural here, but there are still marginalized David Gard, PADC co-president communities, and Piedmont is no stranger to that,” said Lee. “When I came here, I thought about the role I wanted to play, and thought this was a good one — to make the city a more inclusive place, not only for my kids but for all.” Lee received her bachelor’s degree in English from UC Berkeley and a master’s degree in journalism from Columbia University. As an independent journalist for publications including The New York Times, The Atlantic, and Real Simple, she writes about business and technology, parenting and health, and social justice and education. As part of the Asian-American Journalists Association, she also covers Asian-American community stories. The co-presidents have coordinated ongoing events including the annual MLK Day celebration. speaker series, book groups, and a student Art and Writing Showcase, and This year’s MLK Day PADC co-president Ellen Lee. event was attended by over 400 people and featured speakers including social justice activists and Congresswoman Barbara Lee; hip-hop dancers from the Oakland studio New Style Motherlode; and jazz musicians from Oaktown Jazz Workshop. The Appreciating Diversity Film Series at Ellen Driscoll Playhouse was created by the Appreciating Diversity Committee many years ago. It is now co-sponsored by PADC, the city, Piedmont Adult School, and the Piedmont League of Women Voters. “We’ve been around as a nonprofit since 2002,” said Lee. “The hard part for me is the larger scale of the discourse, knowing that nationally there still is some pushback in terms of why this is important.” “For the most part, however, we’re really encouraged. People here do support our mission as a worthwhile endeavor,” added Gard.
articles.title: PADC co-presidents talk about diversity

articles.text: Spanish teachers Deysi Sahagon (left), Viviana Green, and Jessica McMillen, with math teacher Emily Boyes enjoy their lunch, provided by the Piedmont High School Parents Club. Piedmont High School and the PHS Parents Club celebrated its teachers and school employees last week, May 1-5, during its annual Teacher Appreciation Week. The Associated Student Body (ASB) made sure school staff members were celebrated throughout the week. Sophomore class president Genevieve Hiller led the initiative setting up tumblers with tea, classroom gifts, and a pun-themed snack bar. On Wednesday, May 3, the teachers’ lounge was decorated with succulents for staff to take home, and on Friday, ASB members delivered 300 notes high school students had written to their teachers, sharing how much they appreciate them. articles.text: Without play, we cannot find joy or happiness. We need play. But, as adults, almost none of us prioritize play. We calendar in time for exercise and work and we might find ourselves mindlessly scrolling through social media or watching the latest streaming content, but play rarely becomes a conscious choice day to day. Look at your calendar right now and see if you can find any evidence of prioritizing play. Are there portions of your day blocked out for meaningless fun? Socialization with no practical purpose? Games and activities that are not for the betterment of anyone or anything? The benefits of play include connecting with your creative self, noticing the world around you and appreciating beauty, finding enthusiasm, hope for the future, laughter, stress reduction, improving mood, connecting with others. Dr. Stuart Brown, founder of the National Institute for Play has identified eight different types of play personalities. Do any of these resonate with you? For most of us, it will likely be more than one. The Joker: Play is about nonsense or foolishness. Clowning around, funny noises and jokes Adults find joy and happiness through play. are this person’s fun. The Kinesthete: The ones who move and push their own physical selves for fun. Hikers, skiers, yogis, acrobats, dancers, basketball players are all kinesthetes. The Explorer: Play is about discovery both in the physical, intellectual and spiritual realms. The Competitor: For the competitor, the fun comes from competition and the battle to WIN! The rules matter because it gives the structure for the competition. The Director: The organizers who throw the best barbecues or plan the group camping trip. The Directors are planners and create exquisite experiences for themselves and others. The Collector: The collector likes to acquire and search for items within a specific category and/or collect specific types of experiences. The Artist/Creator: Play for this person is creating something artistic or functional. From building robots to painting or sculpting, the artist/creator is driven to make. The Storyteller: The storyteller lives in his or her imagination. Either by writing or creating worlds or inhabiting them through watching theatre, movies or reading novels, this person finds their play through the magic of story. It’s quite likely that you find play in a number of these categories. Being aware of them will help you identify what kind of play you can pursue. It’s time to bring play back into our day. Even in small amounts. And play that connects to creativity, has the power to change our mood, change our minds and change our meaningful relationships. Nina Meehan is the founder of GoCreate (https://gocreate.zone/) which offers services in consulting, coaching and workshops in creativity and communication.

articles.text: Last week Piedmont school kids enjoyed multiple sessions of P.E. class on the Linda Beach pickleball courts. The Linda Beach courts are currently available for pickleball use by the schools and the public during a several month trial being conducted by the Piedmont Recreation Department. At the end of the trial, the City will decide [on] whether [to] use the Linda Beach courts exclusively for pickleball. Pickleball is the nation’s fastest growing sport. The International Federation of Pickleball currently has at least 70 member nations and is striving for inclusion of pickleball as an Olympic sport, possibly as early as 2028. According to the Sports Fitness Industry Association’s 2022 Pickleball Report, a third of pickleball players are under age 25. Former Piedmont High School and professional tennis player, Brad Gilbert, recently told ABC News, “I do see the sport [pickleball] growing because of the much quicker learning curve to play.” Brad Gilbert coached the former tennis great Andre Agassi, who has now become a pickleball convert. According to a recent article on Parents.com, part of the huge rise in pickleball participation is due to the increased inclusion of pickleball in schools’ athletic curriculums and at summer camps. In another article, soccer star Alex Morgan noted that 70 percent of kids in the U.S. stop playing sports by age 13. Morgan urged the prioritization of funding for municipal infrastructure allowing for low-cost participation by kids in sports that are “fun.” Pickleball meets both criteria. Municipalities across the nation are racing to meet the growing demand for pickleball facilities. The Piedmont Pickleball Committee hopes happy youngsters enjoying pickleball at the Linda Beach courts will become a star on a future Piedmont High School Pickleball Team. articles.text: Long wins 800, Sorensen-Wald wins pole vault, boys win 4x400 relay Piedmont High’s track and field team produced impressive results at the 2023 Western Alameda County Conference Championships at Hayward High on Wednesday and Friday, May 3 and 5. PHS qualified in 37 events for the North Coast Section Bayshore Championship on May 13 by attaining top-six finishes or qualifying times. Leading the successful day was senior Parker Long, who won the 800-meter run with a time of 1:55.92 in a field of 45 runners. “I’m feeling good, I’m glad that I can prove I have it still. I was the top seed going into it and it still feels new to have the eyes on me,” said Long. As the favorite, Long feels like there’s been a target on him since running a fast time of 1:53.25 at the Dublin Distance Fiesta on March 18. “I got pretty nervous during the second lap [on Saturday]. I felt super tired and a lot of people were hanging with me. With about 200 [meters] to go, I just launched a kick,” he added. Long is hoping to peak at the right time with the big endof-season meets coming up – Bayshore NCS Meet of Champions on May 19-20 at Dublin HS, and the CIF State Championship on May 26-27 in Clovis. Only seconds behind Long in the 800 was teammate and classmate Christian Taylor, whose time was 1:56.25. Taylor also placed second of 47 runners in the 1600 with a time of 4:20.63 in an exhilarating race with Berkeley’s Mason Mullen, who stayed on Taylor’s back heels until the final corner, kicking his way to the front. “No one really wanted to take the lead, so I took it upon myself to do it. I was ahead for most of it, just trying to get on pace for 4:20. Ultimately, I got outkicked in the last 50 meters,” Taylor said. Taylor recently committed to continue his running career at UC Davis. “It’s nice to have my choice made. It was a bit stressful to wonder if I’m going to run in college. He won the pole vault with a height of 11 feet even, was third of 13 in the 110- meter hurdles in 16:64 seconds, and was fourth of 22 in the 300 hurdles in 42.12. articles.text: Eleanor Lavin was selected to play in the U.S. Lacrosse’s NorCal Senior All Star Game on May 21 at Tamalpais HS in Mill Valley. Piedmont’s girls’ lacrosse team saw its season come to an end on Tuesday, May 2, losing to No. 4 seed San Marin 15-5 in the opening round of the Division 2 North Coast Section playoffs. Piedmont was the No. 13 seed. “The girls are a second-half team, and this time, the hole going into halftime was a little too deep to overcome. We had a lot of trouble gaining possession and controlling the ball,” explained PHS coach Carlton Chan. The match closes the Highlanders’ season with an 8-8 overall record. The Highlanders were able to challenge for the Western Alameda County Conference title once again but fell narrowly 11-9 to Bishop O’Dowd on April 27. “Our goal this year was to challenge in the league tournament. I’m really proud of how hard this team played and the grit they showed against some really good teams,” said Chan. Piedmont also played San Marin earlier this year, which the Broncos won 16-6 on April 1. The Highlanders will lose five players to graduation: Molly Ashton, Lindsay Kottle, Eleanor Lavin, Sofia Johnson, and Holland Feinberg. Lavin recently earned honors by being selected for the U.S. Lacrosse’s NorCal Senior All Star Game on May 21 at Tamalpais High School in Mill Valley. articles.text: Piedmont High’s baseball team closed its regular season on a high note, defeating Arroyo in its final two games. Piedmont won 3-2 in San Lorenzo on Wednesday, May 3, and won at home on Friday, May 5, with a comfortable 11-6 score. PHS closed its regular season on a four-game winning streak and finished with a 12-10 record, including 4-6 in the Foothill Division of the Western Alameda County Conference. The team now awaits its seeding in the Division 4 North Coast Section playoffs. Piedmont honored its three seniors on Senior Day on Friday: infielder Michael Aikawa, outfielder Ryan McConathy, and outfielder Liam Campbell. 11-6 over Arroyo Both teams scored four runs in the first inning, and Piedmont went ahead 5-4 following the bottom of the third, and 10-4 by the fifth inning. The Dons scored twice in the top-of-the-sixth, but the Highlanders scored one more run in the sixth for the 11-6 victory. Trailing 4-0 after the top-first, Piedmont got their bottom half started with Aikawa drawing a walk, followed by Markos Lagios smacking a double to center field. Peter Krumins walked to load the bases, then Dimitri Papahadjopoulos singled in Aikawa, then Will Parker hit a two-run single to score Lagios and Krumins, but Papahadjopoulos was thrown out at third. McConathy then slugged a double to center, and John Olsen tied the ballgame at 4-4 with a sacrifice fly to score Parker. In the third, McConathy hit a oneout single followed by Olsen drawing a walk. With two outs, Aikawa lined a single through the hole at second base to bring in McConathy, 5-4 Piedmont. In the fourth, McConathy hit a one-run single to score Krumins, who led off with a single. Liam Campbell scored the game-winning run in Piedmont’s 3-2 win over Arroyo. Piedmont honored its three seniors on Senior Night on May 5. Pictured are coach Eric Olson (left), Ryan McConathy, Michael Aikawa, Liam Campbell, and assistant coach Evan Haarz. Photos by Mark Aikawa Michael Aikawa had five hits and three doubles in a two-game series with Arroyo. Papahadjopoulos, who walked earlier, then scored on an error by Arroyo’s second baseman after McConathy stole second base. Diego Delventhal then singled in McConathy for an 8-4 lead. Piedmont’s two runs in the fifth came from a double by Krumins to score Aikawa. Aikawa also brought in Piedmont’s last run on a double to center field, scoring Olsen. Final stats: Aikawa was 3-for-3 with two doubles, two RBIs, two runs scored, and a walk. Krumins was 2-for-2 with three runs scored, an RBI, and two walks. Papahadjopoulos was 1-for-3 with a run scored and two RBIs. Parker was 1-for-3 with two RBIs and a run scored. McConathy was 3-for-4 with a double, RBI, and two runs scored. Olsen was 1-for-2 with an RBI and run scored. 3-2 over Arroyo Wednesday’s game was much closer. The Dons led 1-0 until Piedmont tied it in the top of the fourth inning. PHS followed with runs in the fifth and sixth innings. Piedmont opened the fourth inning with three walks from Papahadjopoulos, McConathy, and Delventhal. With one-out, Piedmont executed a successful triple steal. PHS went ahead 2-1 in the fifth after Krumins hit a double to center field, followed by Papahadjopoulos’s two-out single to score Krumins. With the game tied 2-2, Piedmont scored the game-winner with two-outs in the top of the sixth after Campbell hit a single and Aikawa slugged a double to deep center field, enabling Campbell to score all the way from first. Seve Sanchez entered as Piedmont’s closer, retiring three of four hitters by way of a ground out, lineup, and then Sanchez picking off Arroyo’s runner at first to end the game in a pickle. Final stats: Aikawa was 2-for-4 with a double and an RBI. Krumins was 1-for-3 with a double and a run scored. Papahadjopoulos was 3-for-3 with a run scored. Campbell was 1-for-2 with the game-winning run. NEXT UP Piedmont (12-10 overall) waits for their seeding in the Division 4 North Coast Section postseason. The opening round is scheduled for Wednesday, May 17, the quarterfinals are on Saturday, May 20, semifinals on May 24, and championship round on May 26-27.

articles.text: Photo by Erin Callaghan Piedmont’s volleyball season came to an end with loss to Acalanes in the North Coast Section Quarterfinals. Piedmont boys’ volleyball team’s season came to an end on Thursday, May 4 in the quarterfinals of the post-season North Coast Section playoffs. Piedmont lost in three sets to No. 3 seeded Acalanes in a match in Lafayette. Piedmont, the No. 6 seed, fell by scores of 26-24, 25-18, and 25-22. “The boys fought so hard during the game,” said PHS coach Mariah Cardenas. “The first set we kept a lead throughout the set but unfortunately the unforced errors held us back from winning. I always tell the boys it is us versus us, not us versus the – Piedmont volleyball coach Maria Cardenas team across the net. Our serve-receive was fairly strong but our defense was not prepared for the speed of Acalanes. The boys honestly did everything they could, and they should be very proud of themselves.” The match concluded a successful season for the Highlanders with a 14-7 overall record and its second consecutive NCS quarterfinals appearance. “It was bittersweet. This year has exceeded all my expectations. This group of young men is truly the dream team. We worked so hard all season to make it where we did,” Cardenas. For this year’s seniors – WilStaff Photo Outside hitter John Champion will be a senior leader on next year’s volleyball team. Staff Photo Senior Wilson Wong was a major part of the revival and success of Piedmont’s boys’ volleyball program. son Wong, James MaNguyen, Brayden Day, Owen Kelly, Eric Olaru-Hagen, Kai Lambert and Jonas Kra-Caskey – the growth of the program is something they hold near-and-dear. Wong helped revive the program in 2020 prior to the Covid pandemic, helping the team improve from a 3-5 record in the shortened 2021 season. Finishing at 7-8 in 2022, they qualified for the North Coast Section playoffs and upset No. 5 Analy in their first post-season match. “It’s been a massive journey. Three of us were on the B-team in middle school and we always felt like the underdog for seven years. But every single year we improved. We have a really special group,” said Wong. Coach Cardenas took the lead role this season after working as an interim coach in 2022. “Piedmont may never see another senior class like this group,” she said. “These boys truly paved this path from nothing. I’m honored to be closing out another historic season with Piedmont. I hope we can continue to flourish.” Looking ahead to 2024, Piedmont will return significant talent to the lineup. Outside hitter John Champion will lead the group, and junior Shunji Higashi made strides as a setter this season. Freshman Albert Bellingrath entered as a starter during the season and should make a big jump as Piedmont’s main middle hitter.

articles.text: Jasper Schuetz wins Freshman race The Piedmont Mountain Bike team wrapped up its season with the NorCal High School Cycling League Championship on Saturday and Sunday, May 6-7 at Six Sigma Ranch in Lower Lake, sending 17 riders to compete. The NorCal Championship was on a 5.1 mile course with an elevation gain of 750 feet. Jasper Schuetz won the Freshman Division 1 race to finish his season undefeated in five races. He is now the Norcal Freshman champion. Schuetz finished with a time of 41:49.93 over his twolap race. He finished 2.14 seconds ahead of Ryder Williams of Woodcreek High School. In the Varsity boys’ category, Andres Roberts finished 37th of 51 riders on the four-lap course. Also competing was Aleksi Valkonen. In the Junior Division, Max Rivera finished 16th of 84 racers with a three-lap time of 1:08:24.23. Matteo Scanu placed 22nd, Mark Hsia was 30th, Griffin Stein was 62nd and Artun Duransoy was right behind him. In the Sophomore Division, Cary Ward finished 64th, ahead of teammate Ethan Becker. articles.text: Reservations for Stern Grove Festival concerts will be open to the public beginning May 18. The festival begins June 18. All concerts are free, but reservation is required. Headlining the 86th season is The Flaming Lips, with performances by Indigo Girls, Santigold, Lyle Lovett, Bob Moses, and Patti Smith. San Francisco Symphony will perform on July 23. Concerts run from June 18 to August 20. Stern Grove Festival Association is a non-profit organization whose mission is “to make live musical experiences accessible to all.” Since its inception in 1938, the organization has presented the Stern Grove Festival as free concerts in Sigmund Stern Grove, an outdoor amphitheater located at 19th Avenue and Sloat Boulevard in San Francisco. The amphitheater is owned and operated by the City of San Francisco. The natural amphitheater is surrounded by giant eucalyptus, redwood, and fir trees and has become the home of one of Northern California’s most well-attended summer concert sites. The festival has brought more than eight decades of performing arts - including opera, theatre, and music - completely free. articles.text: Let’s all say hello to our new friend, Pennywise, the clown When I was 11 years old, my dad took me to see a sci-fi film titled The Thing. I was simultaneously riveted and terrified. There was one scene in which the Thing, an enormous, manlike creature from another world, stood on one side of a door and two scientists stood on the other side, debating about turning the knob. It’s a familiar trope now, but for me, a kid whose imagination could slip into overdrive at even the prospect of walking down the stairs into a dark basement, that moment to this day remains unforgettable. I think of it as the meta-creepy, hair-raising sweet spot. It’s a place where our labyrinth of fears resides – fears that can define part of our childhood. And it is in this sweet spot that Stephen King resides, coming at it from a myriad of angles with a prolific talent that seems without end. Regardless of the novel of the same name, King is able to find that cluster of fears that reside within the reader/filmgoer and provoke them until fear morphs into dread, most times with astonishing quickness. It’s why standing on the top step of a dark basement, the ominous smells wafting up, then turning on the light switch and finding that the lights aren’t working, is such an effective preview of ominous things that lie ahead. Therein is the power and effectiveness of the film It, made in 2017. Using the image of the benign and joyful clown, King takes the expected and transforms it into something most frightful. Part of the brilliance of this film, set in the small town of Derry, Maine, in 1989, is that it opens with seven middle-schoolers, all just released from school with the summer stretching before them. At the outset they are not a crew, though each resides on that outcast edge of the school experience. They slowly come together and tentatively share their individual encounters with a shape-shifting clown called Pennywise (Bill Scarsgard). In fact, the initial set up of the movie begins with Bill Denbrough (Jaeden Lieberher) constructing a small boat made out of heavy paper for his younger brother, Georgie (Jackson Robert Scott), who wants to go outside and play in the rain and float the boat in the water-filled gutters while he chases behind. That is until the boat disappears into a storm drain and, of course, Georgie kneels down and looks into the opening. Guess what? There, holding the boat, is Pennywise. What is also immensely important is that Pennywise begins to represent those moments of disbelief and then terror, eliciting from the kids their personal anxieties and apprehensions and unresolved fears that will remain with them for a lifetime. Realize that you are not watching a horror film per se. Though King is thought of as a master of the genre, it’s a shallow definition. Know that it is not Pennywise who is at the center of the story. It is the kids, as a group and as individuals, that give this film its essence and texture. Each is dealing with a standing-at-the-top-of-the-basement-stairs moment. Summoning up massive amounts of will each takes one step then a second into that space defined by their own imaginations. The novel It is over 1,000 pages long and is divided into two parts. This film adaption focuses on the kids; it’s also subtitled, and while the end credits roll, it is titled Chapter One. In the denouement of Chapter One, the seven stand in a circle and take a blood oath, swearing to return to Derry if ever need be. And return they do. Not to face Pennywise (it was never about Pennywise), but to finally face their unresolved fears. It. Directed by Chase Muschietti. Starring Jaeden Lieberher, Jeremy Ray Taylor, Sophia Lillis. 2 hrs., 15 min. Rated R.
articles.title: It – scary film but exceptionally well-made

articles.text: Earwig and the Witch is a story about a fearless young orphan who was left to grow up in an orphanage called The St. Morward’s Home for Children, nestled in the bucolic English countryside. Earwig, though rambunctious, is content at St. Morward. She has a best friend, Custard (Logan Hannan), and wishes not to be adopted. She is also unaware that her mother had magical powers. Her life changes dramatically when a strange couple arrives, Bella Yaga (Vanessa Marshall) and Mandrake (Richard E. Grant), who decide to take in Earwig. Puzzled and uncertain, she senses that her new guardians are unusual. articles.text: Alex Roe and Chloë Grace Moretz in The 5th Wave Tweens and teens will find The Fifth Wave compelling considering that it features 16-year-old high school girl, Cassie Sullivan (Chloe Grace Moretz), who has all of her teenage bona fides in place: lots of friends, non-stop texting, is on the soccer team, and is crushing on a senior football player named Ben (Nick Robinson). Based on a Young Adult trilogy by Rick Yancey, the film might qualify for that moniker known as a “chick flick,” had it not been for the fact that it is an apocalyptic/dystopian/futuristic story not unlike Independence Day with an overlay of The Hunger Games. The setup: An average school day, kids in class, all is normal when chilling reports come in that high above the earth hovers a ship of unknown origins. Not just something akin to the Hindenburg floating overhead, but a massive E.T. fortress, one that signals that events are about to take place that will change the lives forever of all those who survive global power outages, earthquakes, tidal waves, a pandemic and finally an invasion. In other words, the visitors don’t come in peace. As her dad (Ron Livingston) explains, “they’re not here for us, they’re here for earth.” Cassie is one of the survivors and she abruptly finds herself alone and on the run. Her father was killed and her mother died of a worldwide flu epidemic carried by birds. Is Cassie resilient? Absolutely. Is the film formulaic and decidedly lame? To the max. Will kids like it? Definitely. End of the world stuff with a small dash of romance. So, while the adults are choosing to stream films such as Tar, Elvis, The Revenant or The Danish Girl, the kids will be eager to see the first installment of The Fifth Wave. The Fifth Wave. articles.text: Paul McCartney (left) and John Lennon The origin of the word skiffle is unknown. In the west of England since the late nineteenth century ”to make a skiffle” means to make a mess of any business. In early 20th century America a “skiffle” was a rent party, designed to pay rent on a house. “Skiffle” was first used on a record in 1925 with Jimmy O’Bryant and his Chicago Skifflers. It was used to describe country blues, including “Hometown Skiffle” (1929) and “Skiffle Blues” (1946) by Dan Burley & His Skiffle Boys. Ma Rainey used it to describe her repertoire to rural audiences. The term “skiffle” disappeared from American music in the 1940s. In the 1950’s, a British skiffle revival developed out of the postwar jazz scene, moving toward traditional jazz. It was acoustic music played by working class people. Notable artists were Lonnie Donnegan, Bill Bailey Skiffle Group and Ken Colyer’s Jazzmen. Donegan’s fast-tempo version of Lead Belly’s “Rock Island Line” was a hit in 1956, selling over a million copies. The root players of British rock were skiffle players, including Van Morrison, Mick Jagger, Roger Daltry, Jimmy Page, Keith Richards, Brian May, Robin Trower, David Gilmour, Graham Nash and a working class bloke from the seaport of Liverpool, John Lennon. John started the skiffle group The Quarrymen in 1957. In addition to skiffle music, they also played a lot of American rock and roll. Within months, Paul McCartney was added, then George Harrison in 1958. Paul replaced Stuart Sutcliffe on bass in 1961. Richard Starkey, better known as Ringo Starr, was added in 1962. John Lennon, Stuart Sutcliffe and Cynthia Powell, then Lennon’s girlfriend, came up with a name variation of The Crickets, Buddy Holly’s band, Initially the band was called The Beatlals, then The Silver Beatles, then finally The Beatles. McCartney grew up in a rich exposure to jazz and popular music. His father James led Jim Mac’s Jazz Band in the 1920’s and played piano at family holiday gatherings. Paul didn’t read music like his dad, and learned by ear and by watching his dad play. Eventually, Paul would take over playing at the family gatherings. “[Paul] provided a lightness, an optimism, while I would always go for the sadness, the discords, the bluesy notes,” explained John Lennon some years later. “There was a period when I thought I didn’t write melodies, that Paul wrote those and I just wrote straight, shouting rock ‘n’ roll. But, of course, when I think of some of my own songs- ’In My Life’, ‘This Boy’-I was writing melody with the best of them.” Listen to and read my 17 Lennon-McCartney Beatles solo examples for this column and music for my previous columns at: http://www.guitarimprov.com/ PostColumns.pdf. articles.text: Perhaps no room in the home evokes stronger feelings in homeowners than the bathroom. Whether a primary suite or otherwise, most desire sanctuary, comfort and functionality. If you have a bathroom that isn’t what you want, it’s a great time to explore updating this key space in your home. While primary suites may be foremost, don’t ignore that guest bath and powder room. Floorplan changes, converting tubs to walk in showers and adding extra footage are typical and should only be undertaken with a licensed General Contractor. For all but the most simplest upgrades, your project will require a permit, which can take several weeks to obtain, and you’ll need drawings. California is subject to regulations such as Title 24, which is designed to ensure that building design and construction maximizes energy and water efficiency. Updated plumbing fixtures, lighting, paint and a new vanity top may be all you need. articles.text: Sabrina Santoyo takes over as owner of Art Loft Framing Many Piedmonters are familiar with Art Loft Framing, the second-oldest business in Montclair Village. Now owned by Sabrina Santoyo, she sat down with the Piedmont Post to discuss her history with the business and her own experience in the picture-framing industry. Art Loft was founded by Tom and Celeste Brodehl 50 years ago, in 1973. Santoyo has worked with the Brodehls for the past 15 years and became the sole owner this year, 2023. The Brodehls first established Art Loft across the street from the current location. “The old location was upstairs and in an actual loft, hence the name,” Santoyo explained. Even after the Brodehls moved the business to its current groundfloor location on Antioch Court in 1984, they kept the name. While Celeste is fully retired, Tom still comes in on Fridays and Saturdays to help facilitate Art Loft’s customer rewards program and “to help me with larger projects,” said Santoyo. “We stay busy here, getting large projects like that about once a week lately. Tom’s the wingspan man.” Working at Art Loft Monday through Friday, Santoyo has had ample time to enjoy and nurture Art Loft’s community of neighboring shops and devoted customers. “Art Loft has been very involved in this community for all of its 50 years,” she said, “and it’s been a joy to continue that tradition where many shops in Montclair Village are clustered. We always put up flyers when our neighbors are having events and promotions.” “The community of our customers, new and longtime, are very invested in the arts — not just framing art. It shows in their care for the pieces they bring and their attentiveness to the work we do.” “There is no typical week,” Santoyo emphasized. Over the course of a few days, framing projects can range from a clasThe exterior of Art Loft. Sabrina Santoyo is the new owner of Art Loft Framing, one of the oldest businesses in Montclair Village. sical Renaissance painting, to a client’s old Boy Scout uniform, to a poster advertising an old sci-fi film, to a beaded purse that a client’s grandmother had purchased in Paris in the 1920s. Born in Los Angeles and raised in Oakland, Santoyo now lives in Concord. As a single mother, she raised a son, Moses, now 21. After six months with Art Loft, a full-time employee with the Brodehls left the business, and Santoyo was hired to take her position. “When I came on it was the recession and it seemed nobody was hiring for a full-time job at all,” said Santoyo. “I’ve been in the picture-framing industry for over 25 years now, and I’ve been grateful every day for the opportunity to continue to pursue it at Art Loft.” “I admire Tom’s work so deeply that I want to stick to his vision for Art Loft,” she said. “According to growing demand from our loyal customers, I’d like to expand our offerings to include some higher-end readymade frames; right now, we only offer custom-built.” The interior of Art Loft, with a vast collection of frame samples on display.

articles.text: If you have a family member with special needs, you might face emotional and physical issues, but you also may be concerned about maximizing the financial support your loved one requires. Consequently, you may want to consider establishing a special needs trust. This type of trust can help maintain the financial security and lifestyle of an individual with special needs. Furthermore, a special needs trust can allow the trust’s beneficiary to receive financial support for supplemental needs without losing public benefits, such as Supplemental Security Income (SSI) and Medicaid. Here’s how it works: You, as the trust’s grantor, establish the trust and name a trustee who is responsible for managing the trust. You can fund the trust with gifts throughout your lifetime or from other sources, such as inheritances or court settlements. But another popular funding mechanism is life insurance, which the trust can purchase on the life of one or both parents of a special-needs child. And as long as the trust is also named the beneficiary of the policy, government benefits will be protected. In a special needs trust, the role of trustee is important. Sabrina Santoyo takes over as owner of Art Loft Framing By Selen Ozturk Many Piedmonters are familiar with Art Loft Framing, the second-oldest business in Montclair Village. Now owned by Sabrina Santoyo, she sat down with the Piedmont Post to discuss her history with the business and her own experience in the picture-framing industry. Art Loft was founded by Tom and Celeste Brodehl 50 years ago, in 1973. Santoyo has worked with the Brodehls for the past 15 years and became the sole owner this year, 2023. The Brodehls first established Art Loft across the street from the current location. “The old location was upstairs and in an actual loft, hence the name,” Santoyo explained. Even after the Brodehls moved the business to its current groundfloor location on Antioch Court in 1984, they kept the name. While Celeste is fully retired, Tom still comes in on Fridays and Saturdays to help facilitate Art Loft’s customer rewards program and “to help me with larger projects,” said Santoyo. “We stay busy here, getting large projects like that about once a week lately. Tom’s the wingspan man.” Working at Art Loft Monday through Friday, Santoyo has had ample time to enjoy and nurture Art Loft’s community of neighboring shops and devoted customers. “Art Loft has been very involved in this community for all of its 50 years,” she said, “and it’s been a joy to continue that tradition where many shops in Montclair Village are clustered. We always put up flyers when our neighbors are having events and promotions.” “The community of our customers, new and longtime, are very invested in the arts — not just framing art. It shows in their care for the pieces they bring and their attentiveness to the work we do.” “There is no typical week,” Santoyo emphasized. Over the course of a few days, framing projects can range from a clasThe exterior of Art Loft. articles.text: A solid turnout of 27 walkers and three K-9 best friends showed up at the Exedra last week on May 3 for some exercise with the Walking on Wednesdays group. The group’s submission of the mulberry trees in front of the Piedmont Play School in Hampton Park had been selected as Heritage Trees by the Piedmont Park Commission on Arbor Day. Mulberry trees had been planted in Piedmont during the 1870s in an effort to produce silk at a “Silk Farm” in the area that is now Littlewood Drive. Mulberry leaves are the only source of food for silk worms. Jennifer Jones provided some background information on the subject for the walkers, with some help from the pre-school students at the Play School. At the Arbor Day celebration, the Play School and Walking on Wednesdays received Heritage Tree pins as awards, so the group wanted to pay a visit to Ritchie and the Play School. The walkers headed off following a usual route, going up Highland Avenue to Sheridan, Wildwood and Crocker Avenues. The group enjoyed seeing the beautiful spring flowers, including rhododendrons, azaleas, California poppies, wisterias, and dogwood. The walkers went up Crocker to Hampton Avenue and past Crocker Park. There was a tree covered with messages of appreciation as part of the City’s annual Michelle Ritchie with Piedmont Play School students Jolene Groboske, Parker Giammona, Sophia Fedor, and Grant Ng-Wilson. invitation to share messages of gratitude on trees throughout the city. The group continued up Hampton to Hampton Park, where they could hear children behind the Play School. Michelle Ritchie and other teachers were supervising play activity, and she and four students agreed to visit with the walkers. After presenting another Heritage Trees pin to Ritchie, it was time for students to get back to play and the walkers to get back to their weekly walk. Before leaving Hampton Park, the group checked out the two tennis courts and the Guy Saperstein Basketball Court with Tyson Lake hidden above it up the hill. The pace on the return to the city center was different, and a long line of them arrived at different times around noon at the Community Hall parking lot. A couple of raindrops fell, but the walkers’ charmed weather lives continued. articles.text: Last month on April 26, the Piedmont Police Department launched its new “Safety 4 Seniors” program. Coordinated by Officer Tyler Petit, the program provides resources to seniors including everyday safety advice, education about phone and online scams, and home security update support. “The program kicked off last October,” explained Petit. “Around that time we started getting more cold calls about seniors facing scams and security problems; at least 60-70% of these issues were preventable given the right safety education. I submitted a memorandum to Chief Jeremy Bowers wanting to create a program providing advice to seniors to prevent them from being victims to these preventable problems, and it was soon approved.” Alongside home security and scam safety presentations during senior meetings at the Community Hall, the program is a new way to provide personalized contact between seniors in Piedmont and the officers serving them and their city. Petit gave a 90-minute presentation and question-and-answer session on April 6 at a meeting with 30 seniors. “I designed the program wanting seniors to know that they can contact PPD and request a one-on-one meeting with other officers or myself to address any safety vulnerabilities they may be facing personally or in their own home,” said Petit. One major resource that the program offers is direct access to the Alameda County Adult Protective Services system. “For seniors in need of home safety or medical assistance – like installing a handicap ramp or establishing easily accessible emergency contacts – who don’t know where to start or are struggling to find help through their own health provider, we can connect them with these services quickly through the county,” said Petit. “Our community policing is strong here in Piedmont, and a lot of our attention focuses on resources for children and younger groups,” he added. “Seniors have had such rich experiences that I think many people assume they have a thorough knowledge of the safety issues they’re vulnerable to, but they didn’t grow up in a time of cryptocurrency assets and gift card scams.” To learn more about the Safety 4 Seniors program or to utilize its resources, contact Officer Tyler Petit at 420-3005 x3241, or by email at tpetit@piedmont.ca.gov.

articles.text: The First Mondays Reading Group met in the Community Hall on May 1 with a turnout of 15 readers for the discussion. An update was provided on a new reading group Bob Hall has created that will focus on short literary works. It had a nice toein-the-water start last week in a Zoom call, with seven people sharing ideas about works by Raymond Carver, Nora Ephron, and Emily Dickinson. The new group will meet on the third Monday of the month, May 15, at 1:30 p.m. Those interested should contact Bob Hall at bmkjhall@comcast.net. The discussion on May 1 centered on The Killer Angels, a 1974 historical novel by Michael Shaara that won the Pulitzer Prize for Fiction in 1975. The book depicts the three-day Battle of Gettysburg during the American Civil War in July 1863, and the days leading up to it, as the Union and the Confederacy troops moved into battle position around the town of Gettysburg, Pennsylvania. The novel is character-driven and is told from the perspective of different individuals in both the Confederacy and the Union. A film adaptation of the novel, titled Gettysburg, was released in 1993. The book’s title comes from Union Col. Joshua Lawrence Chamberlain, one of the novel’s major characters. He remembers reciting to his father a speech from Hamlet: “What a piece of work is man ... in action how like an angel!” But his sergeant replies, “Well, if he’s an angel, all right then...But he damn well must be a killer angel.” Confederate General Robert E. Lee is leading his army into Pennsylvania. He hopes by threatening Washington, DC he will draw the Union army into battle, crush it, and bring the war to an end. However, his most important general, James Longstreet, is gravely concerned. The Union forces are strongly entrenched, and he tries to persuade Lee twice that the Union’s position is too strong. He urges Lee to march away and fight later on more favorable ground. But Lee orders two different attacks on the Union positions. Longstreet follows orders. General George Pickett leads a charge, but is turned back with heavy losses, and the Confederate attacks are repulsed. A shaken Lee orders retreat. Most members of the reading group liked The Killer Angels. They enjoyed the descriptions of the characters and how Shaara developed them. The book is fiction but reads like non-fiction. Readers said they could feel how tired and hungry the soldiers were. The huge death toll – over 50,000 men in three days – and how it was gruesomely described saddened some readers. Equally sad was the fact that these were Americans fighting other Americans, and often friends fighting each other. Some readers found the battle maps Shaara provided to be helpful to follow the military action, but others found them hard to read and confusing. Another issue for some was that it was hard to follow the many different characters Shaara presented. The question of historical accuracy was raised, but unanswered. Shaara did significant research for the book, and considerable amounts of first-person Civil War documents exist. It was noted that Shaara wrote two other Civil War novels. The readers considered the mindset of soldiers needing to follow orders, even when they knew the direction was flawed. The group felt The Killer Angels was a worthwhile read, and a book most readers would not have read were it not for the First Mondays Reading Group. Future discussions The readers had previously selected The Hare with Amber Eyes by Edmund de Waal for June, How Beautiful We Were by Cameroonian-American novelist Imbolo Mbue for July, and Four Fish: The Future of the Last Wild Food by Paul Greenberg for August. The group’s next discussion will be on Monday, June 6 at 1:30 p.m. at the Japanese Tea House in Piedmont Parl. New readers are welcome to join the group and there is no fee to participate. articles.text: Oakland Museum to host first NINS event No Immigrants No Spice (NINS), a Bay Area nonprofit focused on awareness of immigrant contributions through food, culture and economy, will hold its second BBQ without Borders event on Saturday, May 13 at Oakland Museum from 5:00-9:00 p.m. The event will feature Chef Ron Dumra of Wah Jee Wah, Chef Lilly Duran of Clandestina Cafe, and Chef Tadayuki of the former Family Cafe, who will celebrate their regional specialties of Lechon, Tandoori and Yakitori. Guests will be invited to explore the theme of “cultivating home” through physical mini marts constructed in the museum’s gardens. There will also be an area for kids’ activities with a continuous game of “found object soccer”, a basmati rice bag race, an immersive collaborative art piece and a silent auction of premier prizes. Craft cocktails, mocktails, wine, and beer will also be available, and additional food and drink will be available for purchase. Guests may purchase a VIP ticket and donate directly to the Resilience Fund. A sliding scale option will make tickets more accessible to the public. One major resource that the program offers is direct access to the Alameda County Adult Protective Services system. “For seniors in need of home safety or medical assistance – like installing a handicap ramp or establishing easily accessible emergency contacts – who don’t know where to start or are struggling to find help through their own health provider, we can connect them with these services quickly through the county,” said Petit. “Our community policing is strong here in Piedmont, and a lot of our attention focuses on resources for children and younger groups,” he added. “Seniors have had such rich experiences that I think many people assume they have a thorough knowledge of the safety issues they’re vulnerable to, but they didn’t grow up in a time of cryptocurrency assets and gift card scams.” To learn more about the Safety 4 Seniors program or to utilize its resources, contact Officer Tyler Petit at 420-3005 x3241, or by email at tpetit@piedmont.ca.gov. articles.text: Viki Cebers passed away on April 30, 2023, in Walnut Creek after courageously battling a lifetime of health issues. Viki was born December 8, 1947, in San Francisco to Donna Donald and was adopted and raised by Irma Sue and Wilfred Schlieman in Piedmont. She attended Piedmont schools, where she met and later married her high-school sweetheart and love of her life, Hank Cebers, Jr. They enjoyed 32 happy years together before Hank’s passing in 2000. Viki lived for her family and was always looking forward to the next vacation to Graeagle, where she loved seeing everyone together – reading on the porch, working on puzzles and playing cards. Her love for her family fueled her fierce determination and will to live despite her extraordinary health challenges. Her no-nonsense attitude and unique sense of humor helped her fight through incredible physical pain and beat medical odds countless times. Viki is remembered for her selfless contributions to the community. Together with Hank, they were very involved in the Piedmont community, volunteering their time and talents to Piedmont schools, the Piedmont Community Church, the Campfire Girls, and Camp Augusta. Viki was also very active with the fundraising Viki Cebers, a native Piedmonter, died on April 30 at age 75. branches at Children’s Hospital Oakland, both as a member of the Teak Branch for more than 40 years and as the office manager at the branch headquarters until she retired in 2017. Through her service and years growing up and then raising her family in Piedmont, Viki built life-long friendships that kept her energized and inspired her wit. Viki is survived by her three devoted daughters, Mindy Smyth and Michael, Suzy Sims and Josh, and Samantha Cebers and fiancé Aaron. She is also survived by five loving grandchildren, Braden, Parker, Andrew, Jenna, and Carly; her beloved brother Robert Schlieman and wife Bonnie, and her new-found sister, Moire Donald and husband Jeff. Additionally she is survived by two faithful sisters-in-law, Ilze Birznieks (Janis), and Sandra Forderer (Curt), and many nieces, nephews, great nieces and great-nephews. Friends and family are invited to celebrate Viki’s life at a memorial service on Monday, May 15, at 11 am at Piedmont Community Church. In remembrance of Viki’s life, the family suggests making a charitable donation to: Children’s Hospital Branches, Inc., 5700 Martin Luther King Jr. Way T-2, Oakland, CA 94609, with the memo “in honor of Viki” on the check.

articles.text: Members of Girl Scout Troop 33587, sixth graders from Piedmont Middle School, headed out on their most challenging backpacking trip yet. The group hiked three miles to Morgan Territory Backpack Camp near Mt. Diablo on March 11-12, passing through oak groves and grass-covered hills and climbed over and under numerous trees that had fallen during recent storms. Wildflowers were blooming in abundance, including California poppies, larkspur, purple sanicle, Chinese houses, and Mount Diablo sunflowers (endemic to the Bay Area). As they approached the campsite, they saw many cows grazing in the fields. The campsite itself was an idyllic spot with beautiful views of Mount Diablo in the foreground. Once at camp, the girls set up their tents, hammocks, and a kitchen area. They had planned their meals ahead of time, making sure to carry lightweight food. They learned how to filter water and took turns cooking. Indeed, some would say that the form of government the Bible advocates is a theocracy. Others note that the problem with a theocracy is that, without God (theos) physically present, there are many who are far too ready to step in and act like God on God’s behalf. Our Baptist forbearers were cautious about the idea of monarchs and they were resolute in their belief that they should not be given religious or spiritual authority. The concept of king as “defender of the faith” with the authority to appoint archbishops and bishops was morally repugnant to them. It is one of the reasons they became Baptist in the first place. The bottom line is that our religious tradition is very much against giving too much power to any single person or institution. It has long resisted giving political authority to religious leaders as well as giving religious authority to political leaders. King Charles III would like to be known as the “defender of all faiths.” I appreciate his concern. However, history shows that the faiths of the world generally need to be defended from falling into the hands of political leaders more than they need to be defended by them.
